name: Kaviratna and Bhishagratna verse numbering against the standard editions
description: The only public-domain English translations of the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas number their verses differently from the modern editions every paper cites. This records every equivalence between the two that this project's concept corpus states, so a passage read in a free translation can be cited in the form scholars use.
method: Every equivalence here is one the concept record itself states in the text a reader sees. Nothing is computed, and no offset is carried from one verse to another. Each was extracted by a judgement pass over the source fields and then re-checked by a second adversarial pass that defaults to rejecting; only rows that pass are published. Equivalences the source hedges are published separately as hedged rather than given a verse number.
limits: This is not a complete concordance of either text. It covers only the passages this project happens to cite, and the marker counts below are a ceiling found by keyword: a citation that mentions the standard numbering can be counted mechanically, but "this citation has no standard equivalent anywhere" cannot be, and is not claimed.

rejected.problem: equivalenceStated=true but the source field does not state that Kaviratna's verses 7-9 equal '22.4, 22.9-22.12a and 22.44'. The verse field reads '22.4, 22.9-22.12a and 22.44 (standard Trikamji numbering); the definitions printed as verses 7-9 by Kaviratna': the standard loci list covers the whole citation, while 7-9 is tied only to 'the definitions'. 22.4 and 22.44 are not asserted as equivalents of Kaviratna 7-9 anywhere in the field (criterion 1). The standard range is recorded as [?-?], so the digits cannot be matched against the source (criterion 2).

Rule 5 (offset given where the sides are not comparable) and Rule 2 (range does not match the source). The verse field itself says the quoted span is 'aphorism 13 plus the opening sentence of aphorism 14' and that 'the whole quoted span sits inside a single prose sutra, Ca.Su. 28/7'. That is a many-to-one relation: two Kaviratna aphorisms (13 and at least the start of 14) fall inside one Trikamji sutra, so no per-verse offset exists. Publishing offset=-6 would lead a reader to map Kaviratna 14 to 28/8, which the source contradicts (14's opening is in 28/7). The translatorRange [13-13] also drops the aphorism-14 portion the source and the claim's own sourceWording both include; the source span is 13 to (part of) 14, not 13 alone. Minor: sourceWording is a composite paraphrase ('Kaviratna aphorism 13 plus ... (Kaviratna's numbering, Sutrasthana 28, printed pp. 395 to 396)'), not a string present verbatim in the field, though its parts are. Chapter 28, translator Kaviratna, stated=true and hedged=false are all correct; the row fails only on the offset and the range.

Rule 7 (and rule 2). The source record's translator field is 'none; Sanskrit original, out of copyright', not Kaviratna; the claim names Kaviratna as the translator. The Kaviratna figures appear only parenthetically inside the verse field of a Sanskrit-original citation. Additionally the source says '12 and 16' and '14 and 18' (two discrete verses each), but the claim encodes them as continuous ranges [12-16] and [14-18], which asserts 13-15 and 15-17 that the source never mentions.

Rule 7. The source record's translator field is 'none; Sanskrit original, out of copyright', not Kaviratna; the claim names Kaviratna as the translator and marks the row usable. The equivalence 24-28 = 26-30 is already carried by n=6, whose record does name Kaviratna; this duplicate row rests on a record that cites no translator.
